note: Goals and Dreams, content v3 (16 words). Category Emotions & Psychology, course level B1.1 (Gateway level 9), unit Goals and Dreams.

words.meaning: To make something you want come true by strongly believing in it and focusing on it every day (popular self-help idea); also, to show something clearly.
situations: Every morning, Lina writes 'I will get into medical school' ten times and truly believes it will happen.
Omar wrote his dream salary on a note, read it every day, and says that's how he got the job.
gaps: She believes she can ______ her dream job by thinking positively every day.
Write your goals down and repeat them — that's how some people try to ______ success.
His stress began to ______ itself as headaches.
hints: Make a wish real by believing in it strongly — or show something clearly.
Starts with 'mani-' and ends with '-fest'.

commonMistakes.sentence: I'm manifesting to get a new car.
commonMistakes.why: 'Manifest' takes a direct object: manifest something.

words.meaning: A strong promise to keep working at something, even when it's hard, and the time and effort you give to it.
situations: Sara has gone to the gym at 6 a.m. every day for a year, even in winter.
Ali promised his team he'd stay until the project was finished, and he never missed a meeting.
gaps: Learning a language takes time and ______.
Her ______ to her studies impressed all her teachers.
Marriage is a big ______ — think carefully.
hints: Your promise and dedication to keep going.
The noun from 'commit'; has a double 'm' and one 't' before '-ment'.

commonMistakes.sentence: He showed a big commitment for the team.
commonMistakes.correction: He showed a big commitment to the team.

words.meaning: A person who wants everything to be perfect and isn't happy with anything that has even a small mistake.
situations: Mona rewrote her one-page essay seven times because one sentence didn't sound exactly right.
My boss redid the whole slide because the logo was one millimetre too far to the left.
gaps: She's a ______ — she checks her work ten times before she sends it.
Being a ______ can make you slow and stressed.
As a ______, he hates handing in anything with tiny errors.
hints: Someone who wants everything 100% perfect.
Ends in '-ist'; the trait is '-ism'.

commonMistakes.correction: She is a perfectionist. / She is very perfectionistic.

words.meaning: To create a clear picture of something in your mind, like imagining yourself reaching a goal.
situations: Before the race, the runner closed her eyes and pictured herself crossing the finish line first.
Before every exam, Omar imagines himself calm, opening the paper and knowing every answer.
gaps: Close your eyes and ______ yourself on the stage, speaking with confidence.
Athletes often ______ winning before a big match.
It's hard to ______ what the room will look like with new furniture.
hints: Picture something in your mind.
Starts with 'visual-' and ends with '-ize'.

commonMistakes.sentence: I visualize to win the race.
commonMistakes.correction: I visualize myself winning the race.
commonMistakes.why: Use 'visualize something / yourself doing something' — not 'to do'.

words.meaning: A sign that clearly shows something exists or is happening; also, the act of making a wish come true by believing in it.
situations: Ali's hands shake and he can't sleep before every exam — clear signs of his stress.
Lina says her new job is the result of writing her dream down and believing in it every day.
gaps: Headaches can be a physical ______ of stress.
The protest was a ______ of people's anger.
She believes her success is a ______ of her positive thinking.
hints: The noun of 'manifest': a clear sign, or a wish made real.
Ends in '-ation'.

commonMistakes.sentence: His anger was a manifest of stress.
commonMistakes.correction: His anger was a manifestation of stress.
commonMistakes.why: The noun is 'manifestation'; 'manifest' is the verb.

words.meaning: To try very hard for a long time to achieve something difficult.
situations: Sara worked two jobs and studied every night for years to become a doctor.
The small team keeps trying to make their app better every single week.
gaps: We ______ to give our customers the best service.
She ______d for years to become a pilot.
Always ______ for excellence, not perfection.
hints: Try very hard for a long time.
Rhymes with 'drive'; past tense 'strove'.

commonMistakes.correction: He strives for success. / He strives to succeed.
commonMistakes.why: Use 'strive for + noun' or 'strive to + verb'.

words.meaning: Giving a lot of time and effort to something because you truly believe in it.
situations: Omar has volunteered at the animal shelter every Saturday for five years and never misses a day.
The coach comes early and stays late every day because he really believes in his team.
gaps: She's a ______ teacher who stays late to help her students.
He is fully ______ to his family and his work.
We need ______ volunteers who will come every week.
hints: Describes someone who is dedicated and loyal to something.
The '-ed' adjective of 'commit' (double 't').

commonMistakes.why: Spell it with double 'm' and double 't': committed.

words.meaning: The habit of wanting everything to be perfect and being unhappy with any small mistake.
situations: Mona's need for every detail to be flawless means she never finishes her projects on time.
Ali spends three hours choosing one photo because none of them feel good enough.
gaps: Her ______ makes her work slowly.
______ can lead to stress and burnout.
He's trying to let go of his ______ and accept 'good enough'.
hints: The trait (not the person) of wanting everything perfect.
Ends in '-ism'.

commonMistakes.why: 'Perfectionism' is the trait; 'perfectionist' is the person.

words.meaning: To keep doing something even though it is difficult or other people tell you to stop.
situations: Ali failed his driving test three times, but he kept practising and took it again.
The company said no to her idea twice, but she kept asking until they listened.
gaps: If you ______, you will succeed in the end.
He ______ed in asking questions until he got an answer.
Don't give up — ______ and keep trying.
hints: The verb: keep going despite problems.
Starts with 'pers-' and ends with '-ist'.

words.meaning: Describes a person who keeps trying and doesn't give up easily; also, a problem that continues for a long time.
situations: The salesman called me every day for two weeks until I agreed to meet him.
I've had a cough for a month that won't go away.
gaps: Be ______ — send the email again if they don't reply.
She's very ______ and never gives up on her goals.
He went to the doctor because of a ______ headache.
hints: The adjective: describing someone or something that keeps going.
Ends in '-ent'.

words.meaning: The quality of continuing to try even when things are difficult.
situations: It took Edison thousands of failed tests before his light bulb finally worked.
After 50 rejections, the writer's book was finally published.
gaps: Success comes from hard work and ______.
Her ______ finally paid off when she got the job.
Learning to code takes patience and ______.
hints: The noun: the quality of not giving up.
Ends in '-ence'.

commonMistakes.why: Use the noun 'persistence' as the subject.

words.meaning: The moment when an important change happens and things start to go in a new direction.
situations: After meeting an inspiring teacher at 16, Omar stopped skipping school and decided to study medicine.
Losing her job pushed Sara to start her own business, and her life changed completely.
gaps: Moving to London was a ______ in my career.
The second goal was the ______ of the match.
Becoming a father was a real ______ in his life.
hints: The moment everything starts to change.
Two words: '___ing' + a word for a moment or spot.

commonMistakes.sentence: It was a turn point in my life.
commonMistakes.correction: It was a turning point in my life.

words.meaning: Money that criminals demand before they will free a person they have kidnapped.
situations: The kidnappers called the rich family and asked for a million dollars to let their son go.
Hackers locked the company's computers and asked for bitcoin to unlock them.
gaps: The kidnappers demanded a $1 million ______.
The family paid the ______, and the boy was freed.
The hackers asked for a ______ to unlock the files.
hints: Money paid to free someone who was kidnapped.
Rhymes with 'handsome'.

commonMistakes.sentence: They paid a ransom of the kidnappers.
commonMistakes.correction: They paid a ransom to the kidnappers.

words.meaning: Feeling low, sad and without energy for a while, often without a clear reason (informal).
situations: Since the holidays ended, Lina has stayed in bed, skipped the gym and doesn't feel like seeing friends.
After losing the final, the team was quiet and unmotivated for a whole week.
gaps: I've been ______ all week — I can't focus on anything.
He's been ______ since his girlfriend left.
A walk outside can help when you're ______.
hints: Feeling low and unmotivated for a while.
Three words: 'in a' + a word that is also a music style.

commonMistakes.why: The phrase needs 'a': in a funk.

words.meaning: Lending money at unfairly or illegally high interest rates.
situations: The man lent his neighbour $100 and demanded $300 back a month later.
Some loan apps charge 400% interest, trapping poor people in debt.
gaps: Charging 200% interest is ______ and is illegal in many countries.
The loan shark was arrested for ______.
Many religions forbid ______.
hints: Lending money with crazy-high interest.
Starts with 'usu-'.

commonMistakes.sentence: He made a usury to his friend.
commonMistakes.correction: He charged his friend usurious interest.
commonMistakes.why: 'Usury' is the practice; 'usurious' is the adjective.

words.word: Get your foot in the door
words.meaning: To get a first small chance in a job or organization that may lead to better things later.
situations: Sara took a low-paid internship at a big bank, hoping it would lead to a real job there.
Omar started as a receptionist at the TV station and is now a news reporter.
gaps: The salary wasn't great, but it was a good way to ______ of my career.
An internship can help you ______ at a big company.
Take any job there — you just need to ______.
hints: Get a first, small chance that can lead to more.
An idiom about a body part and an entrance.

commonMistakes.sentence: I got my leg in the door.
commonMistakes.correction: I got my foot in the door.

collocations: get your foot in the door
